newsitem.title: USA: Xerox may struggle to find Talegen buyers.
newsitem.headline: Xerox may struggle to find Talegen buyers.

text.p: Xerox Corp may have a hard time finding buyers for its five Talegen insurance units after buyout firm Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co's surprise decision to walk away from a $2.7 billion deal to buy the entire group.

Industry analysts say the deal appears to have unraveled due to an actuarial dispute over reserves and concerns about deteriorating industry fundamentals since KKR struck the deal with Xerox in January.
KKR's decision to call off the deal also could have a chilling effect on other property-casualty insurance deals.
Xerox will not say why the deal was called off and said it believes that the reserves for its various Talegen units are adequate and that the companies are healthy. KKR declined to comment.

The Stamford, Conn., document processing company also said it was prepared to sell the Talegen group in pieces and still expects to get about the same price for the businesses that KKR had agreed to pay.
But the news drove Xerox shares down more than five percent, or 3-1/8, to 54-3/4 in mid-afternoon trading.
The insurance industry has been one of the biggest participants in this year's booming corporate merger market and this deal was among the industry's largest.

"This transaction is interesting because it could mark the beginning of a shift in the other direction, in which it's no longer quite such a sellers market, and in that respect it would have implications for other deals and for stock valuations," Oppenheimer analyst Alice Schroeder said.
Although other potential KKR targets could benefit from the collapse of this deal, it still may send a negative signal about the industry, Lehman analyst Peter Wade said.

"I think any time you have a big deal like this (that falls apart) that's going to have a negative impact on other deals," Wade said. "I don't think it's a good day for mergers and acquisitions in the insurance industry as a whole."
Although Xerox is likely to find buyers fairly quicky for one or two of its Talegen units, the others -- especially Crum & Forster -- would be a tough sell, analysts said.
Crum & Forster, a middle market commercial insurer, wrote a substantial amount of asbestos and environmental coverages and has little to attract prospective buyers, analysts said.
"Crum and Forster is in the most competitive part of the insurance industry with only limited competitive advantages," Wade said.
Xerox will find a buyer for it, he said, but the question will be at what price.

But Xerox's professional liability insurer Coregis was likely to attract a buyer quickly, analysts said. Its workers compensation insurer Industrial Indemnity and its excess and surplus lines insurer Westchester Specialty also may be fairly marketable, analysts said.

The remaining piece is The Resolution Trust Group, which manages the claims and reinsurance collection on various books of the insurance group's discontinued business and has minimal premiums because it writes no new business.

"Intuitively it is going to be somewhat difficult for them to sell it in individual pieces because, as always, there will be buyers for the more attractive parts and there won't be buyers for the less attractive parts," Schroeder said.
"There's obvious buyers for some pieces like Coregis," she said.
But, she said, "it is not insignificant that terms that were acceptable to KKR nine months ago no longer are."

"We believe the insurance environment has deteriorated during that timeframe," she said, and therefore is not inconsistent with KKR's decision last month to sell its majority stake in American Re Corp to Munich Re.
KKR earlier said it was still interested in the property-casualty insurance business.
Schroeder said KKR might still be a buyer of insurance assets at the right price.
But, she said, "their timing of insurance acquisitions has been stellar and I think people should take note of this."
